text: You assume people's psychological resistance to increased cost is entirely based on the proportional impact of those cost increases. Yes, housing/gas/groceries are much larger portions of the increase in cost, but datacenters are much more visible than poor foreign policy or starting new conflicts with overseas energy producers. Also, electricity traditionally has much less cost variation than gas/housing/groceries. At my company's internal conference we had a rep from one of our partners come speak, and he emphasized that a significant value-add of our company's relationship to our partners is that we're much more tech-forward. he went on to say "Execs in [partner industry] don't know what AI is or what it does, but they know that they want it." We're seeing AI features being bolted into every application under the sun, whether it actually adds functionality or not. I think you bear a significant burden of proof to the claim that the demand for datacenters is in turn driven by consumer demand for AI, and company boards losing their minds over what they think AI can do and demanding their R&D divisions sink millions of dollars into AI spend to try and capitalize on their dreams. I'm reminded of Bitcoin: for a hot minute every startup was talking about blockchain and GPUs were getting snapped up by miners left and right because of what people imagined the value could be. That's what I'm getting at when I say "shareholder value:" these developments seem to be less about what value a company is _actually_ producing (& thus the inherent cost-of-goods-sold demand), and more about the _possibility_ of what value a company _could_ produce.

And of course approvals become a bottleneck, but they also catch bugs. My job has legal compliance products, so we have an extensive QA & testing process which a "YOLO ship slop" approach won't work for.

Maybe I should tell another story. I wanted originally to be a graphic designer, as a kid spent years in Paint and PaintShop Pro, finally learned Photoshop. I tried to intern with a graphic designer and he basically said "you don't want this job", it was already competitive and becoming automated. I was not such a versatile illustrator and was better at layout, I joined newspaper and learned InDesign and Pagemaker while at a place that still laid out classifieds by hand. I remember when my Editor's older brother came in who worked at Time with a digital camera and said, "We don't develop photos anymore, and we can even send them in from the field." I believed in journalism but the tech side of it for me, a dead end. Only a few people were needed now for the production. So I learned web development, cut my teeth on Internet Explorer and DHTML. We hated the fight between browser behemoths, why couldn't they agree on a standard? Well, they did. And now, anybody who could read a standards doc could do my job. So, I moved on to app development. Apps were exciting — still are! — now I could make a program and see people use it in their hand in their daily life. Many competing technologies, Android seemed like the right choice, open core so the ecosystem thrived. A few years in, this also meant anyone in the world with a basic subsidized phone and a computer that could run Java could do my job. I switched mostly to iOS. I think you see where this story is going, but I agree with the article. We fight for equal access to knowledge and tooling. Information wants to be free! And I see that firsthand every day. That is — to reference TFA — a double-edged sword. As we share information we lose control of it. Is AI the potential greatest success of open-source or its failure? I think we still have time to decide if we make the right choices.

Rant: For work, I've mostly given up on using LLMs for large features, in all cases I've tried in the last 2 years, the time it takes to clean up their output is about the same I would have spent writing and debugging the feature myself. There's only a single major feature I've shipped that was mostly written by an LLM, and that was back in May. All other major tasks I've tried, even somewhat trivial ones, led to unusable code, filled with comment slop and workarounds, and hidden bugs. This is probably due to the sheer amount of legacy code our app has, but even trying to develop more or less self-contained components was very difficult. Most of my current job is now going over PRs submitted by my team members, that are mostly all AI-generated, and cleaning them up. The amount of junk inserted into the code by current SOTA models is astonishing, especially during rounds of bug fixes, probably due to context rot. Hundreds of useless variables and small wrapper functions on top of wrapper functions. Hundreds of comments that are essentially word salad, or worse, the LLM talking to the user through the comment instead of through the chat, essentially saying in a comment "I was a good subservient model, and did what you wanted! This function now returns an error, see?". Repeated hundreds of times. Not to mention actual bugs that the inane and lazy unit tests it adds never catch. I'm far less lenient on AI output than on if the same dev wrote the code herself. Thankfully, people in my team cooperate with me and fix my comments, and so far we have no pressure from management to move faster. /Rant Nitpick: Title seems to be missing a word: "Are you USING a subscribed LLM or a locally open-source model". One of my core pieces of advice to AI leaders who get interested in biology is "do not say you will cure cancer, the medical establishment will immediately write you off as clueless". Instead, I recommend AI people say "we believe our new technology will be able to rapidly make significant improvements to the detection and treatment of cancer. We will work closely with medical researchers to help them use our tools effectively." When I did my own cancer research ~25 years ago, the only treatments were basically chemo or radio therapy. The outcomes were often terrible- even for people who lived, they suffered terribly. We are now in a state where new technologies are making absolutely amazing improvements in treatment- with far fewer side effects, which greatly increases quality of life in people undergoing the treatment, and after. I think if we keep grinding on this problem (as well as with many other diseases), we could very well make most cancers a non-death sentence that can be treated routinely with minimal side effects. Here is a thing that did not exist when I was a PhD student: a person with cancer goes to the doctor, they take a biopsy of the tumor and send it to a lab, which sequences the cancer genome. That genome is then input to an AI which understands a great deal about cancer immunology, and spits out a custom antibody which is then injected back into the person, and that antibody teaches the person's immune system to fight the cancer more effectively. There literally is an AI model (my coworkers developed one that is in clinical trials now) integrated in the treatment process, which is absolutely necessary for the high effectivity of the treatment. That knowledge alone inspires me to do my best work, with the belief that it will have positive outcomes. There's another open question- to what extent do we need to understand the underlying biology of cancer, versus having models that integrate enormous numbers of variables effectively to come up with treatments without a mechanistic model. It's quite clear we really do not understand how drugs work (no matter how much publications claim we do), and probably by improving methods by which we can sample the enormous space of potential drugs/treatments. And finally: how can we made this affordable? Cancer treatment in the US is obscenely expensive with many levels of rent seekers who constantly add unnecessary cost to treatment. That will likely require aggressive and intelligent legal regulation (clearly the market is not efficient), and I don't see any sort of political will to make it happen.

Step 2: Prompt the agent to comment out the "when" code and check if the tests fail. (If tests don't fail it's a poor test) Step 3: Prompt the agent to write mutation tests to harden the suite Step 4: Prompt the agent to write property-based tests. Step 5: Prompt the agent for 100% code coverage Step 6: Keep a look out for small issues with steps 2-5 above and refine a Skill or Rule to package the workflow and plug gaps in the model's current shortcomings. Step 7: Dedicate some time to manually reviewing and thinking about interesting edge cases worth testing. --- If you follow these steps, you will have better test coverage than 99.9% of any code an engineer ever wrote pre-AI... and it will be almost completely automated. My team's incidents and bugs are DOWN this year while we're shipping more. Leveraging AI effectively requires a new paradigm of interaction. The name of the game is to use techniques and strategies and guardrails that create an environment that produce good software.

Unless you think that AI will quickly hit a wall (which seems odd considering that only a few years ago the best models had trouble doing basic math or counting the number of Rs in "strawberry"), I don't see how that's reassuring. The models will only get cheaper and more capable over time. It seems quite likely that at some point (probably before I hit retirement age) they'll be able to fully replace me at my job. Is there any specific cognitive task that you are willing to bet that AIs won't be able to accomplish in the next 5 years? Because if not, I'm not sure we're disagreeing about predictions.

I agree, understanding the code does not save us. Knight Capital wrote every line of their code but it didn’t prevent a $440 million loss in under an hour [0]. Regarding wisdom, I do not mean knowledge of how the system works. That is a thing, too, where the person who built it is the only one who understands it. That’s not what I meant here. In the examples of my coworkers, for example, I see at least two things: 1. The things they create are 90% well crafted, 30% well engineered. If they were building a rocket, every part would be well machined to high precision. Then when we assemble the rocket, we find out it’s too heavy to ever get off the ground. That’s a kind of wisdom gap. 2. They work in a way that excludes everyone else on the team. From their perspective, they are wondering why everyone else isn’t getting on board. But it’s a situation where one person understands it, and their deep understanding of it contributes to them moving fast, and then add AI and now the ground is shifting faster than anyone else can understand enough to contribute. This is another kind of wisdom gap, knowing how to get a team performing at a high level, versus an individual contributor performing at a high level. This is where, from your perspective, you’re driving a speed boat as fast as you can, wondering why your coworkers aren’t on board. But from their perspective, they’re following your boat in their boats, but your boat is creating waves behind it and splashing water up, so their experience is a bumpy ride getting water splashed in their face constantly while they’re yelling “hey can you slow down up there?” From your perspective, it makes no sense to slow down. You’re not experiencing any problems. Yet both perspectives are still true. The person who is charging forward as fast as possible also seems to be the one who has less experience operating and supporting systems, understanding how systems fail in unexpected ways, and so forth. Every week I have a conversation where someone tells me, “oh, I didn’t consider it might fail in that way”, and every time I think, yeah it would have been really nice if we’d had a 20 minute conversation 6 weeks ago when you started. In general, it’s not that “other people just haven’t figured out the tools yet”, it’s also a significant part of who’s leading each initiative. I could absolutely do what my coworker does and setup my custom harness to pull off amazing stunts of productivity. I just think it’s irresponsible much of the time. [0] [URL]

I was one of those people until 2013. I kept a Windows Server infrastructure going for about 50 people at a small company. When I took over in 1997, the Email server was a separate box running an obscure program I can't even remember now. (Edit: It was TFS Gateway, from TenFour Systems, running on it's own Windows 98 Box, if I recall correctly) Eventually we migrated to our in house Exchange Server. I kept that, and everything else running for 16 years, through Y2K and all the rest. I wasn't the best IT guy, but I cared, and I was persistent in hunting down problems. I have no idea how they're doing now, but it made sense when they outsourced IT in 2013, because my job had mostly evaporated, because I got things very stable. To me, Outlook will always be that tough as nails program that ran on your laptop or desktop and worked even when you were on an airplane with no connection to the world. It magically synced up to Exchange when you did have connectivity. It was always there, no matter what. Now Outlook is a service, which to me is nuts. They've taken the work of everyone at Microsoft over more than a decade, and thrown it all away, in the name of a bit more recurring revenue. (They did license the Exchange servers, and the OS the Exchange Server ran on, so even that was a recurrent stream of revenue) There are now far, far fewer people watching over everyone's gigabytes of email stored in the deleted items bin as a handy storage file. Some of them are now using Gmail instead. But there are less people who give a shit about email, less people who know how it all really works. Those people now depend on another separate layer of people, the ones who keep the virtual server layer alive, who are now separate from the people who keep the network layer alive, who are now separate from the people who keep power, AC, physical security, etc. all alive. --- That explains a good chunk of why things are failing. I'll also add that we've been dependent on OSs that are unfit for purpose for 30 years longer than we should have been. It's nuts that we're using ambient authority based OSs, instead of things that default to NO, and strictly enforce capabilities provided by batch files and/or user choices at runtime. We could have much better, and more secure OSs without the need for virus scanners, etc... but most programmers and IT folks don't even know that's an option these days. It was people giving a shit that took up that difference, and we're running out of them. This article explains a lot for me, thanks for sharing it. Edit: As stated above, the Email message gateway was TFSgateway, from TenFour Systems. I spent 15 minutes digging with Google to find that... so I guess I still give a shit, don't I?

I've spoken to several engineering leaders who want to better understand their team's AI usage, but don't know where to start. I've also spoken to several engineers who are stuck and don't know how to level up. There's a lot of FOMO building up and being vulnerable about your AI skills is not easy. Adoption metrics like DAU/WAU and token counts tell you who has access and who uses AI tools. While an ok proxy for AI proficiency and productivity, they say very little about what happens inside a session and how engineers and teams actually use AI. Which models get used and were they the right fit for the work? Are we spending consciously? Do tests run before a commit? Do outputs get questioned or accepted as is? Do outputs need a lot of repair or do they just get refined? Are repos missing out on scaffolding opportunities (skills, context files)? How's my team doing in AI competencies like context management, evals, and orchestration? Pheebs captures that and more. It records the shape of sessions and gives engineers a private view of their own work, separate from the team reports. To make sense of the data, Pheebs proposes an AI Proficiency Model, which looks at two things: 1- Repertoire: which harness capabilities show up in an engineer's work across six competencies: models, artifacts, MCP, evals, context management, and orchestration. 2- Judgement (inspired by the Discernment competency from Anthropic's AI Fluency Index): what happens to AI output before a PR is created and merged. Does it get verified, challenged, refined? And was the model used appropriate for the task? Most teams run the largest model for everything. Pheebs shows how much they could save by running smaller models where they fit. Pheebs is open source so give it a try and send us some feedback!

Indeed. Basically every completed step is a git commit of a worklog and a commit of the updated "TODO" list. I have a queue of tasks that have to be done, the agent reads that, does some research, updates the worklog (does not commit), does the work, crosses out the task from TODO, updates the worklog and commits. This started out as a human-in-the-loop setup, but now it mostly just works on it's own. The initial run is in systemd timer+service. So the whole thing mostly runs on it's own. There are multiple skills - for different tasks. If there's a crash, pi restarts (some scripts around that), checks the worklog, sees that it's not committed and assumes that it did not finish, updates are handled the same way. Now the TODO can be wildly different. Read my email, prepare an answer to insurance. Read my email, update my calendar. Figure out and optimize my home assistant automation. Use the ghidra MCP to rev-engineer a crackme.exe. Optimize my Openwrt wifi network (complex topology, multiple APs), rewrite my old java 6 code to modern java with tests, research birthday presents based on hobies etc... So far I've thrown just about everything I could think of into that setup - the only time I actually need to do something is when pi needs me to do something in the physical world - say - a TRV on a radiator got air blocked and I need to bleed it. Or it did the research and I actually need to buy something. I get a notification and a calendar entry. I do have a similar setup at work, but since my company moves at snail pace compared to development outside, this is my way to keep "up to date".

I can mediate with project manager about some requirements which should not be implemented. I can make decisions to simplify the system without bothering my manager with endless details. I can create short and concise report. I can say "no". I can store passwords in the database unencrypted and unhashed. So far AI that I've used failed spectacularly on these prospects. They're like "yes-man". They'll try to do everything you ask of them. Even if you ask nonsense, they'll not push back. They'll go crazy about security stuff, even not relevant to the current situation. They'll complicate the code endlessly for situations which will not arise, making the code an incomprehensible mess. They'll write so many useless words that any reader will forget what this report is about before then reach the middle of it. They'll never iterate on code until it looks good. They'll stop when test pass. They don't have aesthetical sense of beauty. They love to cheat too often. And you can't do nothing about that. You can't fine them or fire them, and they know about it. They're smart but I'm not convinced they're ready to replace human in mundane engineering jobs.

disclaimer: Not the OP. 1. I feel like I have a decent amount of my identity tied up in being "smart". I have always enjoyed learning, have been good at solving problems, and have been able to get out of some pretty difficult circumstances that were definitely slanted against me in terms of being able to find a stable and high paying job through a combination of luck, being born decently smart, and hard work. 2. For my entire life I have been able to work towards or have a job where my purpose is to solve interesting problems and get paid well for it. I have been lucky enough to be in a position where I could paid to sit down and build solutions, understanding every intricate detail of what I made. And now, it seems like the entire industry is just throwing this away. Why engage with deep thought when everyone around is thoroughly convinced that the act of thinking is "last gen" or "going out of style"? If everyone else is wrong, that doesn't change the pressure to just stop thinking and ship 50 commits a day of unread slop. If everyone else is right, why bother thinking? I am just going to lose my job and be stuck doing menial labor until the AGI builds robots that can do my job. Either way I am unhappy. And sure, I do not need to use AI outside of work, but that does not change the existential dread of having the next 30-40 years of my career turned into something that I absolutely hate. Overall, we have effectively built a machine or a widespread perception of a machine that rewards not thinking and not taking responsibility. Why bother trying to accomplish anything if a machine can do it better than you. I value solving problems, I value understanding, and I value working hard, and at least for me I feel that I may have to start mourning the fact that you used to be able to get paid to do all three. Consider the true scope of just this work for any given ecosystem: How would I as an individual developer, or even a CTO at a small to midsize company, justify the investment to fix that? It would take buy-in from a Google-level entity to create and rollout such tooling for, say, Java. Copying a few functions, or even recreating a whole HTTP server from scratch, is a smaller body of work. Sure, I could vendor and keep an eye out for CVEs, that’s a valid approach. But that’s me copying and taking ownership of an external codebase, not taking a dependency. Ownership is easiest for code that you’ve written, because you (or your team) also built the mental model to go along with it. And if I have to vet a new codebase anyway, I’d rather it be the smallest subset that I actually use; not the full functionality of NGINX. I can justify making the locally optimal decision (reimplement some functionality so I can truly own it) and that may result in a less than optimal global outcome. I can’t justify doing to the globally optimal thing at the expense of my company. Ultimately, the incentives aren’t aligned. The activation energy to get from locally optimal to global optimal is too high, and that’s not going to change any time soon. In fact, it’s rapidly trending the other direction. AI makes it easy to reimplement the functionality you need. An idealized view of “if only people paid for high-quality dependencies this would be solved” is not one I can buy in to. That’s not the reality I live in, for better or worse. In a world where nobody wants to shoulder the burden of vetting dependencies, avoiding them is often the best alternative.

I'm not going to lie, to me it's clear: the job has nothing to do with what it was. Developers used to write code by hand, and humans understanding the full logic of a system mattered a lot. Today, with AI, it's so much easier to produce or understand code that this barrier is gone. The new job that's taking shape is very far from where it started. I get that a lot of people find it hard to accept, and even see the change as a bad thing. That's normal: the job won't appeal anymore to people who were, and presented themselves as, technicians and experts. As for me, yes, I clearly understand my codebase less. I'm sure of it, I've noticed it lately. What I tell myself is that my value is less there now, and more in my ability to organize the whole thing, on the human side as much as the machines and tools. So I focused on what actually brings value to my company or my role, and it's true that code counts for less there. I completely understand people who feel lost. A lot of developers chose this job because they were comfortable with code, not to do marketing or sales. And the job that's taking shape asks them to code less and organize more, that's the real tragedy of this shift. Unfortunately that's how the world works: adapt or die. Let's be clear, a lot of people won't make the jump. They'll see their job as dead and may end up leaving it. That's normal, and a shame. But on the other hand, I think believing you can do without AI is limiting yourself, even a bit illogical. As imperfect as it is, refusing to use it is a bit like refusing the printing press when it was invented. Lots of jobs died, that's a certainty: everyone who wrote texts by hand. Honestly, I see AI exactly like the invention of the printing press. It deeply changes how we produce content, and we know we're going to produce a lot of it. With the printing press, as with AI, we produce a lot of imperfect stuff, maybe even pointless texts. We already see it: AI often produces code that isn't secure and leaves holes. But flip the question: what valid reason would we have today to abolish the printing press? It produced millions of mediocre books, and yet nobody wants to go back to scribes, because it put the written word in everyone's hands. I think it'll be the same for AI. The real question isn't that it produces bad code, it's what we'd be willing to lose by refusing to use it.

My sense is that it likely made sense before Campbell's law took effect. IIRC they developed a reputation in the early 2000s for only hiring very bright people who could solve those kinds of problems on the fly. Then 1. the company needed more employees and 2. people started grinding away practicing those problems so they could pass tests that were intended to filter them, and you got what you have now. Lots of other companies cargo-culted them in the meantime and thought the studying was the point, or maybe for them it was (measuring compliance instead of brilliance). Also concurrently I think a lot of HR departments were increasingly trying to create an air of objectivity to reduce legal risk, which is also where you get the N years of experience crap (e.g. my company's HR just made us change wording from something like "strong ability" to "5 years experience" with Go. I don't even have 5 years of Go experience specifically and I'm the technical lead on the team. Actually the way Go's culture is, I wouldn't be surprised if a lot of experience with it were a negative as far as I'm concerned).
